title: Chapter LVII

teacherSummary.text: Mr. Bennet reads Elizabeth a letter from Collins warning against an engagement with Darcy and laughs at the idea, not knowing her feelings. Elizabeth must hide her pain.

vocabulary.definition: A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided
vocabulary.context: “ ‘My motive for cautioning you is as follows.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “caution”: -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Yet in spite of all these temptations, let me warn my cousin Elizabeth, and yourself, of what evils you may incur, by a precipitate closure with this gentleman’s proposals, which, of course, you will be inclined to take immediate advantage of.’
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “closure”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Much as I abominate writing, I would not give up Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “abominate”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from") + min (Latin minor, "smaller") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Collins and myself on this happy event, let me now add a short hint on the subject of another: of which we have been advertised by the same authority.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “advertise”: ad- (Latin ad, "to, toward") + vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Darcy, who never looks at any woman but to see a blemish, and who probably never looked at you in his life!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “blemish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To play or move to and fro
vocabulary.context: If he had been wavering before as to what he should do, which had often seemed likely, the advice and entreaty of so near a relation might settle every doubt, and determine him at once to be as happy, as dignity unblemished could make him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “waver”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “divert”: vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Following as a result, inference, or natural effect
vocabulary.context: It suddenly struck her that it might be from Lady Catherine; and she anticipated with dismay all the consequent explanations.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “consequent”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A thick, black, lustrous, and sticky substance obtained by boiling down tar
vocabulary.context: Could he, or the Lucases, have pitched on any man within the circle of our acquaintance, whose name would have given the lie more effectually to what they related?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pitch”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: I must not, however, neglect the duties of my station, or refrain from declaring my amazement, at hearing that you received the young couple into your house as soon as they were married.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “declare”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: News traveled quickly through gossip networks in the gentry.

significance: Mr. Bennet's laughter is painful dramatic irony.
discussionQuestions: Why can't Elizabeth tell her father the truth?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with pride and self-knowledge?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LVII,” how does Austen show a misguided warning? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LVII, how does Austen develop the idea of a misguided warning? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVII develops the idea of a misguided warning. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LVII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of a misguided warning. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LVII suggests about a misguided warning. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter LVII to complicate the reader's understanding of a misguided warning. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a misguided warning responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LVII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a misguided warning follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LVII and its treatment of a misguided warning. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LVII as evidence for a larger claim about a misguided warning in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a misguided warning. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why can't Elizabeth tell her father the truth? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are cautioning, closure, abominate, advertised, blemish. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““ ‘My motive for cautioning you is as follows.” Webster's says: A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided. Now the word history: “caution”: -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “closure”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “abominate”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from") + min (Latin minor, "smaller") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. News traveled quickly through gossip networks in the gentry. Why does this chapter matter? Mr. Bennet's laughter is painful dramatic irony. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a misguided warning.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: If he had been wavering before as to what he should do, which had often seemed likely, the advice and entreaty of so near a relation might settle every doubt, and determine him at once to be as happy, as dignity unblemished could make him. In that case he would return no more. Lady Catherine might see him in her way through town; and his engagement to Bingley of coming again to Netherfield must give way.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LVII,” how does Austen show a misguided warning? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a misguided warning, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes a misguided warning. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
